input.question: Why don't atoms in a molecule collapse each other's wavefunctions?
input.ground_truth: I think that some of the reason there is such confusion exhibited in the answers thus far is because this is related to a very much unresolved aspect of QM. We could say that, in response to your question, from the postulates of quantum mechanics measurement is the action of a Hermetian linear operator acting on a state vector which yields a real eigenvalue that corresponds to a physical observable. So two wavefunctions (the scalar product of the state vector and the real space position ket) overlapping or interacting doesn't represent such an act of measurement. There is no projection onto eigenstates. But that answer isn't really staisfying, since it just appeals to the postulates. So the best I can do beyond that is refer you to the (measurement problem)[_URL_0_] and point out that I also don't know how the (f & @k magnets work.)[_URL_1_]

messages.content: You are a helpful AI assistant.

Explain the following question in a simple way as if you are explaining to a 5-year-old.

Question: Why don't atoms in a molecule collapse each other's wavefunctions?

Answer:

response.prediction:
Okay! Imagine atoms are like tiny, bouncy balls. When these balls (atoms) get close to each other and make a team (a molecule), they don’t just squish into one spot or get mixed up completely. 

Each ball has its own special “bubble” of where it might be found, like a cloud around it. These are called wavefunctions. If the bubbles just collapsed into one, we wouldn’t know where each ball is, and the molecule wouldn’t work right.

But the balls have rules (like in a game!) that help them stay in their own space most of the time. They don’t want to be in exactly the same spot as the other balls because that would make them feel uncomfortable (this is called the Pauli exclusion principle). So, they keep their bubbles a little separate, even when they are close together in a molecule.

That’s why the atoms’ wavefunctions don’t collapse into each other—they like to keep their own space, just like how you like your own spot on the couch!
